messages.subject: rbind.fill
parts:
Hi all,

I am trying to put together the output of several lme objects, with different estimated models, in a more useful format for analysis and comparison. These outputs included several dataframes of unequal length but with partly matching column names. After many hours working on this without any success I come across rbind.fill, which I believe can do the trick. Yet something is still missing:

> L <- list(model.b=model.b,model.b1=model.b1, model.c=model.c,
+           model.d=model.d,model.e=model.e,model.f=model.f,model.g=model.g,model.h=model.h,model.h1=model.h1)
> L <- llply(L,function(x) summary(x)$tTable[,c(1,2)]) # extract coefs and sds
> L <- llply(L,as.data.frame)
> 
> L <- list(model.b=model.b,model.b1=model.b1, model.c=model.c,
+           model.d=model.d,model.e=model.e,model.f=model.f,model.g=model.g,model.h=model.h,model.h1=model.h1)
> L <- llply(L,function(x) summary(x)$tTable[,c(1,2)]) # extract coefs and sds
> L <- llply(L,as.data.frame)
> do.call(rbind.fill,L)

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: rbind.fill
parts:
Hi:

Thanks again for the dput() output; it was helpful. A str() of the
list showed that each component of L was a data frame. It seemed
reasonable to want to denote the term associated with each row in the
output data frame, so I wrote a small function to do that. The
function is first applied to each list component (the inner llply()
and then the results are concatenated with ldply().

library('plyr')
# utility function
f <- function(d) {
d$term <- rownames(d)
d
}
ldply(llply(L, f), rbind)

The result identifies the model and term associated with each row as
well as the coefficient and its standard error.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: rbind.fill
parts:
If you want printed tables of regression summaries, then look into any
of the following:
(i) the xtable package, which produces tables from output of
certain types of model objects (e.g., lm) and exports to LaTeX
(generally through Sweave) or html;
(ii) the latex() function in the Hmisc package, which generates
LaTeX code to be inserted later into a LaTeX program;
(iii) the memisc package.
There may be others.

xtable contains functions that are designed to render a pretty-printed
table inside a LaTeX document or an HTML document. The latex()
function in Hmisc generates LaTeX code for a given type of table. For
table printing to the R console, the remix package is a reasonable
option, but I wouldn't recommend it for use inside a document; try
example(remix) after the package is installed and loaded to see what
it outputs.

I haven't used memisc yet, but a quick survey indicates that it might
be the most appropriate for your needs, as it appears the package
author is in political science and most of the data sets and examples
in the package are in that area. Several users on R-help have also
recommended it in the past, so it does seem to have a fan base. plyr
is meant for summarizing/organizing/processing data by groups, not
pretty printing, although it's possible to write a function that sets
up the pretty printing inside the function body for export elsewhere
(such as an external file), in which case the plyr function to use
would likely be l_ply().

My suggestion: read the memisc documentation (it comes with a vignette
and demo). Find out at which stage the table is generated by the
appropriate memisc function - i.e., during the model fit or afterward.
Write a function whose input argument is a data frame; fit a model and
call the memisc function that returns the (code to produce the) table.
If you intend to export the (code for the) tables to a list object,
then return the table (code); if you need to export the table (code)
to an external file, then the last line of the function has to be some
type of write function with a file name - there are several ways the
file name could be specified. This might be the trickiest part. Then
use dlply() to output to a list object or d_ply() to export the tables
elsewhere.

Dennis

Hi,

Thank you your detailed email. I am actually familiar with most of the tools you mentioned plus a few others, such as apsrtable(). Unfortunately, none of them take lme objects as inputs. Sorry if my previous emails were unclear but, as of now, I am *not* interested in making pretty latex tables: *any* descend dataframe or matrix displaying the results of several lme models side by side will do. Thus my interested in the *dply functionality. The trick is that these models will provided outputs of different lengths( the number of predictors varies from model to model) and a only partially overlap of the variable names. I am sure your tool can do trick, but I am not just very conversant with it as of now. Actually your code:

dply(llply(L, f) , rbind)

was useful, but would be better to have a dataframe (which doesn't have to be nicely format as long as it is clearly readable), where the models results are displayed side by side. Attached, there is the code and data for a fully reproducible example, with just a fraction of the actual data set, just long enough to make the model run and converge..
 
I really appreciated your time and help,

Antonio.

messages.author: dc06d729e023580a
messages.subject: Re: rbind.fill
parts:
Hi Antonio,

Here's how I'd attack your problem:

option(digits = 2)
models <- list(
model.b = model.b, model.b1 = model.b1,
model.c = model.c,
model.d = model.d,
model.e = model.e,
model.f = model.f,
model.g = model.g,
model.h = model.h, model.h1 = model.h1)

model_sum <- function(x) {
t_table <- summary(x)$tTable
data.frame(parameter = rownames(t_table), unrowname(t_table[, 1:2]))
}

model_sums <- ldply(models, model_sum)
names(model_sums) <- c("model", "parameter", "estimate", "se")
# That form of the data will be easiest to plot.
# e.g.

library(ggplot2)
qplot(parameter, estimate, data = model_sums, colour = model)
qplot(estimate, model, data = model_sums) + facet_wrap(~parameter,
scales = "free_x")

# But if you want a table where it's easier to compare the numbers,
# use reshape2

library(reshape2)
modelm <- melt(model_sums, id = c("model", "parameter"))
dcast(modelm, variable + parameter ~ model)


Hadley
